Unravelling the impact of innovation and continuous improvement in emerging economies Sarfaraz Javeda | Uvesh Husainb | Shariq Mohammedc | Mohammad Shahfaraz Khand | Wafa Jaouadie | Sajjad Nazirf aDepartment of Accounting and Finance, Faculty of Business, Sohar University, Sohar, Al Batinah, Sultanate of Oman. bDepartment of Economics and Business Studies, Mazoon College, Muscat, Sultanate of Oman. cCollege of Commerce and Business Administration, Dhofar University, Salalah, Sultanate of Oman. dCollege of Economics and Business Administration, University of Technology and Applied Sciences (UTAS), Salalah, Sultanate of Oman. eFaculty of Law, Economics and Management Sciences of Jendouba, University of Jendouba, Kef, Tunisia. fDepartment of Management, Faculty of Business, Sohar University, Sohar, Al Batinah, Sultanate of Oman. Abstract This study delves into the evolving influence of Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies on Business Sustainability (BUSU)- driven Organisation innovation (ORIN)in manufacturing, focusing on emerging economies like Oman. While Industry 4.0 holds vast potential, the pathways it affects at BUSU remain underexplored. Our research aims to fill this void by analyzing the combined effects of ORIN and continuous improvement (COIM) approaches on BUSU. Specifically, we investigate how the adoption of I4.0 amplifies these consequences. We apply structural equation modeling (SEM) to the data collected from two hundred manufacturing companies operating in various industries. We aim to dissect the complex links between technological competence, process refinement, and BUSU among these companies. The findings highlight an apparent synergy, indicating that businesses that utilise innovation and continuous improvement strategies report significantly improved economic and environmental performance. In addition, the results of our research indicate that the implementation of Industry 4.0 increases the connection between ORIN efforts and BUSU, establishing it as a particularly important mediator. This work contributes to a deeper theoretical understanding of the role that I4.0 plays in environmentally responsible manufacturing and provides strategic insights for industry leaders and policymakers engaged in cultivating industrial ecosystems that are both resilient and sustainable. Keywords: business sustainability, organisational innovation, improvement and development, manufacturing sector, structural equation modeling 1. Introduction The manufacturing industry has undergone significant changes thanks to innovative technologies that have redefined organisational structures and production techniques. Significant efficiency gains occurred during the first Industrial Revolution, which introduced water and steam-powered mechanised manufacturing. During the Second Manufacturing Revolution, vast production made possible by assembly lines was driven by electricity. Electronics and information technology became indispensable for industry during the third Industrial Revolution—also known as the digital revolution—which helped enable computerised operations and automation (Schwab, 2017). For modern industry, I4.0 marks a fundamental transformation. Using advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, and cyber- physical systems, to create highly interconnected production environments (Lasi et al., 2014), the fourth Manufacturing Revolution is distinguished by the integration of digital and physical systems. I4.0 offers hitherto unheard-of possibilities for intelligent, flexible, effective manufacturing techniques. Real-time data analytics and automation enable companies to maximise operations, reduce waste, and improve output (Kagermann et al., 2013). Still, these changes bring complicated problems. Manufacturing companies must adopt new technologies and creatively organise their activities to remain competitive while meeting the global demand for ecologically friendly solutions. Emphasising the need for manufacturers worldwide to adopt ecologically sustainable practices, the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) stress the importance of adopting practices such as waste reduction, energy conservation, and emission reduction (UN, 2015). By encouraging ORIN and constant evolution, Industry 4.0 offers compelling solutions to business challenges (Stock & Seliger, 2016). There is no straight line road to reach this harmony. Emphasising how I4.0 technologies may enable long-term BUSU goals in manufacturing through ORIN and continuous development, this paper addresses the vital intersection of technological progress and environmental responsibility. COIM and ORIN Due to I4.0, ORIN is becoming increasingly crucial for adapting to rapidly changing technological environments. Characterised by adopting fresh ideas, technology, or goods, ORIN helps companies exploit advanced technologies and satisfy evolving customer needs (Crossan & Apaydin, 2010). Under I4.0, such innovation requires manufacturers to fully leverage technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and robotics (Birkel et al., 2019), thereby transforming their operational frameworks, workforce development, and management approaches. In a sector that is becoming increasingly digital, manufacturers must cultivate a creative culture that supports continuous adaptation, rather than relying solely on new technologies to maintain a competitive edge. While minor changes in Manufacturing processes rely on COIM, ORIN increases general flexibility. Lean and Six Sigma ideas guide constant development toward minimising waste, enhancing quality, and ensuring customer satisfaction through methodical changes (Bhuiyan & Baghel, 2005). This approach helps companies develop resilient and learning cultures, enabling them to capitalise on new opportunities and address emerging challenges. Continuous innovation is essential in the era of Industry 4.0, as new technologies provide real-time data analytics and predictive insights, thereby enhancing decision-making. IoT-enabled solutions enable companies to monitor equipment performance and identify inefficiencies, allowing for quick and effective process changes that reduce resource consumption and downtime. The symbiotic relationship created by the interaction of ORIN and ongoing improvement drives Manufacturing BUSU. While innovation provides the basis for the acceptance of present technology, constant research assures the application of these technologies to improve efficiency and lower waste. Thanks to developments in additive manufacturing—especially 3D printing—complex component manufacture with little material waste has been revolutionised, supporting sustainable manufacturing practices (Ford & Despeisse, 2016). Encouraging resource-efficient practices reduces waste and energy consumption, aligning with BUSU goals. The increasing use of I4.0 technology emphasises the critical link between ORIN, ongoing development, and environmental goals. ORIN is a challenging idea that has been well-investigated in several fields, including management, economics, and sociology. It involves embracing fresh ideas, technology, or products within a company to enhance performance, competitiveness, and flexibility in response to external events (Damanpour & Gopalakrishnan, 2001). Theoretical models of ORIN may rely on Rogers's diffusion of innovation theory (2003), which examines how new ideas and technologies spread within and across organisations. Rogers lists five critical factors that decide the acceptability of innovations: relative benefit, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability. Especially in complex production environments, these components are crucial in understanding how businesses adopt and utilise new technologies. Underlying the need for businesses to adapt to rapidly changing technological environments, ORIN is gradually being recognised as a dynamic capacity within the context of Industry 4.0 (Kooistra, 2020). Dynamic capacity theory holds that businesses must welcome new technologies and become internally flexible enough to reorganise resources, processes, and talents as new opportunities arise. I4.0, where rapidly developing technologies such as IoT, artificial intelligence, and big data analytics ask for continuous organisational agility and adaptability, particularly relates to this point of view. Companies that support creativity and education will benefit from these changes, thereby enhancing their competitive advantage in the context of Industry 4.0. Particularly under I4.0, the creative culture within businesses relies significantly on leadership. Those who welcome risk-taking, experimentation, and cooperation are more likely to design environments that inspire creativity (Garcia et al., 2012). Adopting creative I4.0 technologies relies on such leadership, as the deployment frequently demands that businesses rethink old processes, accommodate new management practices, and upskill their workforce. Effective integration of new technologies relies primarily on leaders who prioritise innovation and are committed to driving change when technological changes are rapid. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Javed et al. (2026) 4 Moreover, outside factors are incredibly crucial in deciding business innovation strategies. Competitive challenges, legislative regulations, and market expectations for BUSU lead manufacturers to grow in ways that manage social and environmental responsibilities. As BUSU becomes a fundamental need in manufacturing, organisations must innovate in energy efficiency, waste reduction, and sustainable supply chain management (Kesidou & Demirel, 2012). Theoretical models incorporating internal and external elements under I4.0 provide a better understanding of how ORIN may be employed to achieve sustainable outcomes in production. To investigate how ORIN could assist BUSU in the manufacturing sector, this paper compiles dynamic capacity theory, the diffusion of innovation framework, and viewpoints on leadership and external forces. It primarily examines how I4.0 technology can enhance social impact, economic viability, and long-term environmental responsibility when adopted in a creative organisational culture. This paradigm emphasises ORIN as the main instrument for addressing the complex possibilities and difficulties given by I4.0, laying a foundation for understanding how manufacturing companies could deliberately adopt new technology to improve BUSU. Grounded on lean manufacturing and Total Quality Management (TQM), constant improvement is a basic tenet in manufacturing. The models show little progress in production methods aimed at increasing operational efficiency, reducing waste, and improving quality, with only slight improvements in manufacturing procedures (Imai, 1986). In traditional production environments, constant improvement typically involves a methodical process analysis, identification of inefficiencies, and the application of small, incremental changes. Projects of this kind are crucial in competitive industries where consumer expectations for BUSU and quality are high and where even minor process changes can significantly affect profitability and performance. Applied constantly, the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle—also known as the Deming cycle—is a fundamental instrument. This iterative approach compels companies to methodically develop improvements, implement them, assess the outcomes, and apply necessary changes (Moen & Norman, 2009). Lean manufacturing and Total Quality Management align well with the PDCA cycle, fostering a methodical approach to problem-solving and cultivating a culture of ongoing learning within the company. Within I4.0, digital technologies, including real-time data analytics, the Internet of Things (IoT), and machine learning, are transforming approaches to ongoing development. These instruments enable producers to track production more precisely and support data-driven decision-making, thereby optimising quality and efficiency (Radziwon & Madsen, 2014). Constant monitoring of equipment performance, made possible by IoT-enabled devices, helps businesses identify problems before manufacturing interruptions occur. Through predictive analytics, this real-time monitoring helps to shift from reactive to proactive management, promoting ongoing improvement to reduce resource waste and downtime. Besides production, I4.0 's constant innovation spans supply chain management, customer service, and product design. Constant improvement plans help companies reduce waste, simplify assembly techniques, and conserve resources, thereby improving business sustainability (BUSU). Optimising logistics helps lower emissions and enhance the resource economy, thus benefiting supply chain management and promoting BUSU. Through I4.0 technology, producers can create flexible, robust, and sustainable systems that dynamically respond to changing market needs and environmental constraints (Jasti & Kodali, 2014). Constant improvement is therefore enabled. In this sense, COIM guarantees efficiency and a path towards sustainable manufacturing. Closely aligned with BUSU goals, I4.0 technologies enable ongoing improvement processes that reduce resource waste and lower energy consumption. This article examines how the enhanced COIM procedures of I4.0 technologies contribute to ensuring long-term sustainability in manufacturing businesses. This paper aims to provide insights on how manufacturers can bring BUSU into the core of their operations by employing continuous upgrades through real-time analytics and predictive capabilities, enabling steady development. Figures introduced by I4.0, often referred to as the fourth Industrial Revolution, a spectrum of advanced digital technologies transforms traditional manufacturing into highly automated, data-driven processes. Among these technologies, Kamble & Sharma (2018) found cyber-physical systems, big data, artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, additive manufacturing, cloud computing, and the Internet of Things (IoT). I4.0 stands out for its capacity to collect, assess, and use enormous volumes of real-time data, enabling companies to optimise production project maintenance requirements and respond rapidly to changing market demands. Employing resource optimisation and waste reduction, this data-driven approach supports BUSU, increasing operational efficiency and promoting BUSU. IoT is essential in I4.0 through connected networks of intelligently communicating devices and equipment. This link enables a system in which autonomous monitoring and administration of Manufacturing processes can be attained, drastically reducing the need for human participation (Wortmann & Flüchter, 2015). For example, real-time equipment performance data acquired by machinery sensors enables businesses to identify problems early on and engage in predictive maintenance. This proactive strategy reduces unplanned downtime and extends equipment lifetime, resulting in cost savings. I4.0 predicts and analyses data using artificial intelligence and machine learning. Artificial intelligence systems can utilise sophisticated data patterns to predict equipment issues, optimise manufacturing schedules, and forecast client demand. Through machine learning, the refinement of these forecasts may increase factory responsiveness and efficiency (Hermann et al., 2016). By flagging out areas of resource waste and energy use, AI-driven analytics may help encourage BUSU by offering actionable insights to lower environmental impact. Often referred to as 3D printing, additive manufacturing is another fundamental technology in I4.0. Unlike conventional manufacturing techniques that can generate excess waste, additive manufacturing, which builds objects layer by layer, utilises only the required components to construct each object. For instance, aerospace and automotive companies are progressively using additive manufacturing to create lightweight, fuel-efficient parts, promoting both environmental and economic benefits. Big data and cloud computing further enhance I4.0, providing the necessary infrastructure and processing capabilities to manage vast data volumes and execute complex calculations. Cloud solutions enable businesses to rapidly store, analyse, and distribute data across multiple locations, thereby promoting integration and collaboration throughout global supply chains. Big data analytics provide more profound insights into operational performance and business unit limits, while cloud computing centralises data storage and analytics, thus allowing for quicker and more effective decision-making (Reuter et al., 2017). These technologies, used together in I4.0, are reinventing production as a highly flexible and responsive system that minimises environmental impact, maximises resources, and reduces waste through their interaction. Still, effective use of these technologies does not ease any difficulties. Many companies—tiny and medium-sized businesses (SMEs)—struggle with high expenses, technical complexity, and the need for trained staff to utilise new digital technologies effectively. This paper examines how businesses can overcome obstacles to using I4.0 technology in ways that improve operational excellence and benefit BUSU equally. This research aims to enhance knowledge of sustainable manufacturing in the age of I4.0 by analysing the role each technology plays in supporting efficiency and resource optimisation. In manufacturing, BUSU refers to working in a way that satisfies present requirements without compromising the capacity of future generations to meet their own needs. Initially proposed by the World Commission on Environment and Development (1987), this idea of sustainable development requires manufacturers to balance their operations' social, economic, and environmental components. Thus, long-term BUSU in manufacturing is a comprehensive method that merges these three pillars into decision-making, directing companies toward responsible resource usage, the lowest environmental impact, and consistent economic viability, which drives them. Environmental BUSU is to minimise the negative consequences of manufacturing on the environment. Reducing their environmental impact involves reducing greenhouse gas emissions, conserving water and energy, minimising waste, and managing product lifecycle (Shrivastava, 1995). I4.0 technologies, including IoT and artificial intelligence, help change our approach to achieving these goals by enabling precise real-time resource optimisation and monitoring. IoT sensors, for instance, track energy use across production lines, allowing companies to identify and rectify inefficiencies; artificial intelligence algorithms optimise operations to reduce waste and pollution. Including BUSU at the centre of operations helps manufacturers address growing legal and societal expectations for environmental responsibility and reduce their environmental impact. Manufacturing social BUSU ensures that companies prioritise employees, communities, and society. This means providing fair compensation, equitable and safe working conditions, and opportunities for skill development and advancement (Elkington, 1997). Social BUSU becomes increasingly essential as I4.0 technologies change the Manufacturing landscape. Questions about job displacement, skill shortages, and employee well-being might develop from the movement toward automated technology and digital processes. These technologies, however, also provide opportunities for safer, less physically taxing offices. Manufacturers can encourage a socially sustainable approach that benefits workers and broader populations by establishing policies that promote workforce resilience and skill development. In manufacturing, economic BUSU is the promise of long-term financial survival for companies that employ enhanced competitiveness, profitability, and adaptability in changing markets. Usually requiring ongoing innovation and improvement, achieving economic benefits helps businesses reduce costs, optimise productivity, and improve product quality by employing this approach. In this sense, I4.0 technologies are highly significant as they enable companies to make data-driven decisions, enhancing operational efficiency and agility (Hart & Milstein, 2003). While advanced analytics improve Manufacturing planning and inventory management, enhancing profitability, predictive maintenance solutions assist in reducing costly downtime. Moreover, financially stable companies are better equipped to support environmental and social goals, as evidenced by economic BUSU. Although I4.0 has significant promise to support BUSU, challenges remain in fully realising its benefits in all domains. For instance, the energy consumption associated with artificial intelligence and data centres might offset the environmental benefits of improved efficiency. Moreover, restricting access, particularly for SMEs, is a high cost and technical difficulty that I4.0 deployment calls for. This paper examines how I4.0 technologies can be integrated into manufacturing processes to enhance long-term business sustainability across the financial, social, and environmental domains. Research Methodology This study utilises I4.0 to explore how ORIN and COIM enhance BUSU, employing both descriptive and analytical research techniques. Including the types of innovations and continuous development strategies employed, the descriptive part notes the current adoption of I4.0 technology in production. Knowing the basis of this approach—capturing the characteristics of the production scene as it is—helps one understand the surroundings in which these technologies operate. On the other hand, the analytical component examines the interconnections and cause-and-effect relationships among innovation, continuous growth, and environmental outcomes. This dual approach clarifies the events and critically examines how various organisational tactics influence BUSU in numerous Manufacturing situations (Saunders et al., 2019). This design helps one see patterns and understand how I4.0 technologies impact general business, resource consumption, and organisational efficiency in the manufacturing sector. This study's population comprises manufacturing companies that utilise I4.0 technology, as these companies are likely to integrate ORIN and COIM techniques required to promote Business-University Synergy (BUSU). This research investigates how the integration of technology facilitates sustainable manufacturing processes, with a focus on companies that actively utilise modern technologies, including IoT, artificial intelligence, and robotics. Selected to represent this demographic, a sample of 200 manufacturing enterprises was drawn from industry directories, databases of Manufacturing manufacturers, and relevant trade organisations. Where I4.0 use is widespread, these databases and directories offer access to companies in several Manufacturing sectors, including automotive, electronics, and heavy equipment. Companies focusing on I4.0 and the BUSU of the study may benefit from this approach. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Javed et al. (2026) 8 Primarily, managers and technical staff working on BUSU programs, innovation, or continuous growth within their businesses participated in the survey. These individuals were selected due to their first-hand knowledge of I4.0 implementation, providing a perceptive analysis of the specific challenges and solutions related to BUSU. Initial contacts were made through business directories or industry networking events, and subsequently, a formal request was made to be included in the study. Responders were advised to complete surveys or attend interviews to ensure both quantitative and qualitative data collection. Selected for their statistical robustness and diversity, the 200-firm sample allowed for the investigation of trends and patterns. Firms are stratified randomly according to industry, size (small, medium, significant), and I4.0 deployment (early, advanced). This stratified approach ensured the representation of important subgroups, thereby allowing the study to compile different perspectives on how ORIN and ongoing development align with environmental objectives. Complex populations were divided into subgroups or strata based on pertinent criteria using stratified random sampling, ensuring a representative sample of the manufacturing population (Saunders et al., 2019). This encourages equitable manufacturing involvement, employing varied businesses, technological proficiency, and Manufacturing expertise. Every group meets the stratum specification; random samples are chosen to guarantee subgroup representation and prevent overrepresentation (Etikan & Bala, 2017). This approach increases generalizability by capturing I4.0 adoption and sustainable practices throughout the Manufacturing sector. This stratified random sample study examined how industry type, technology usage, and company size impact ORIN, steady growth, and BUSU. This approach shows how Manufacturing companies handle I4.0 environmental concerns. To ensure a representative sample (Saunders et al., 2019), this study stratified the population by significant characteristics using stratified random sampling. This approach involves companies of various kinds, technological capabilities, and Manufacturing sectors, thereby encouraging fair participation in the manufacturing industry. I4.0 technical difficulties and resources help organisations of all sizes, from small to large (Etikan & Bala, 2017). Their degree of I4.0 adoption divides businesses even more; early adopters and sophisticated users exist in corporations. From initial integration to advanced deployment, this range enables the research to gather information at various phases of digital transformation. The sample consists of companies in sectors such as automotive, electronics, and heavy machinery, with higher degrees of I4.0 adoption and distinct BUSU problems. Employing stratification by industry type, the research helps to address sector- specific practices and challenges (Kamble et al., 2018). Every group receives random samples chosen according to the stratification to ensure that every subgroup is equally represented, thereby decreasing the likelihood of overrepresentation from any one group (Etikan & Bala, 2017). By representing the diversity of I4.0 adoption and BUSU practices throughout the Manufacturing sector, this method strengthens the generalisability of the findings. Stratified random sampling benefits this study by considering variance across critical dimensions—company size, technology adoption, and industry type—that affect ORIN, ongoing development, and BUSU results. This method enables the study to examine how manufacturing companies address the promises and challenges of I4.0 for BUSU. This research utilises primary and secondary data to explore how the adoption of I4.0, organisational innovation, and COIM help manufacturing realise Business-User-System-User (BUSU). Primary data are collected through semi-structured interviews, which include BUSU, continuous education, corporate innovation management, and technical staff. Structured questionnaires were used. The research assessed the types of innovation, the acceptance of I4.0 technology, and the business value of the results. Survey tools were assessed using recognised metrics and indicators from innovation and BUSU research (Bryman, 2016), ensuring consistency and reliability. Based on the survey findings, the interviews provide a qualitative analysis of various corporations' I4.0 technology integration problems, opportunities, and business strategy goals. This mixed-strategies approach demonstrated how various methods contribute to achieving both quantitative and qualitative aspects of sustainable production. Secondary information from white papers, case studies, and trade publications supported the main data results. These websites helped the core data analysis and improvement process by offering a perceptive study of industry standards, benchmarks, and general trends. The study strengthened its findings by utilising secondary sources and provided an outsider's perspective, enabling comparisons between specific businesses and broader industry practices (Nguyen et al., 2021). 3. Calculated means, standard deviations, and frequency distributions provide the attributes of the data from a moment-in-time viewpoint. This initial study provides the basis for further statistical testing and, thus, early insight into how these factors interact with BUSU by aggregating the degrees of creativity and constant improvement across the selected companies. The SEM analysis provides a comprehensive view of the interconnections between innovation, COIM, and BUSU. The mediation analysis within SEM confirms that COIM partially mediates the relationship between innovation and BUSU (indirect effect Beta = 0.68, p < 0.001). This suggests that the impact of innovation on BUSU is enhanced when firms adopt COIM practices. The moderation analysis (multigroup SEM) shows that industry type moderates the relationship between innovation and BUSU. Specifically, the effect of innovation on BUSU is more substantial in the electronics sector compared to the heavy machinery sector, underscoring the role of sector-specific dynamics. Particularly in line with I4.0, the results of this study highlight the vital role organisational innovation and COIM play in enhancing the Business-University of Science and Technology (BUSU) of the manufacturing sector. These findings support earlier research that highlights the importance of modern technologies and a commitment to process improvement in achieving long-term success (Manavalan & Jayakrishna, 2019). Companies can significantly enhance the environmental performance and efficiency of their manufacturing operations by incorporating creativity into their ongoing development strategies. Studies on investments in organisational innovation reveal that companies that incur these costs are more likely to provide better BUSU outcomes. This aligns with the findings of Awan et al. (2019), who argue that reducing resource consumption, thereby minimising environmental impact and promoting innovation, drives sustainable development. I4.0 technologies, such as IoT and additive manufacturing, enable companies to optimise production procedures and reduce waste. Through these modern technologies, businesses can streamline procedures and reduce their environmental impact (Luthra & Mangla, 2018). Moreover, our findings suggest that the impact of creativity on BUSU transcends just technological advancements to encompass necessary organisational reforms. A sustainable manufacturing strategy primarily encourages creative culture, restructuring initiatives, and new business models (Albort et al., 2018). These organisational adjustments provide the tools required to integrate and safeguard the ideas generated by I4.0, fostering BUSU and ongoing development. The report emphasises the strategic need to merge ORIN with improvement projects. These elements provide a solid foundation for environmentally friendly manufacturing. Based on SEM studies, complete innovation and ongoing development are the most significant routes to BUSU. Constant innovation improves environmental performance and maintains competitive advantage, claims Vafaei et al. (2019). The implications are significant for manufacturers. Companies that want to fully realise their potential for BUSU must give ongoing improvement culture high importance along with technology adoption. This dual attention will be vital as businesses strive to reduce their environmental impact while remaining competitive globally. Adopting new technologies alone might not be sufficient; supporting an organisational culture that stresses continuous process improvement ensures that innovations are constantly maximised, allowing for long-term business success. This study demonstrates that companies must combine ORIN with COIM strategies to achieve sustainable outcomes in an I4.0 context. Based on the strategic insights from this research, BUSU projects should be comprehensive, encompassing both the gradual development of existing systems and the adoption of new technologies. This approach offers a scalable and adaptable architecture that enhances existing operations, supporting resilience and flexibility in the face of future technological advancements and evolving environmental needs. 4. Conclusion This study, under the I4.0 paradigm, has examined the transformational potential of ORIN and continuous manufacturing industry development to promote long-term business sustainability (BUSU). By combining analytical and descriptive research methods, we demonstrated that, in manufacturing, achieving long-lasting outcomes relies on creativity and continuous improvement. Our findings suggest that businesses that combine modern technologies with a solid commitment to process optimisation are far better equipped to reduce environmental impact, increase operational efficiency, and fulfil their social responsibilities. This study provides a fundamental realisation: combining I4.0 technologies—notably the https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Javed et al. (2026) 12 Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and additive manufacturing—as facilitators of sustainable innovation has a primary advantage. Long-term BUSU depends on these technologies, helping companies maximise resource use, reduce waste, and increase manufacturing efficiency. However, I4.0 innovation combines organisational changes with the adoption of technology. To support a company's BUSU commitment and prepare for future challenges, it includes adjusting business models, simplifying processes, and encouraging innovation and experimentation. Furthermore, this paper emphasises the need for updates to BUSU standards. Lean and Six Sigma provide continuous efficiency and resource optimisation by employing a logical development framework. To reach technical innovations, innovation must continually be improved. This combination reveals that Manufacturing BUSU calls for objectives and cultivating a culture of continuous improvement. The integration of innovation and development lays a dynamic foundation for environmentally friendly manufacturing. While constant development guarantees their integration and improvement over time, innovation brings fresh BUSU tools and concepts to life. This dual approach enables companies to address environmental issues and adapt to developments within their sector. For companies that practice BUSU, these results are noteworthy. To compete globally, companies must emphasise technical innovation and process improvement. This calls for a plan that sees success and innovation driven by BUSU rather than an expense. Changing their perspective to value innovative technologies and ongoing research enhances operational resilience, long-term business sustainability, and profitability. In I4.0, sustained production depends on constant development and organisational creativity. Companies with a focus on innovation will be best positioned to meet the growing needs of stakeholders, consumers, and regulators. According to this study, these two factors provide a strong foundation for BUSU, enabling companies to meet their social, financial, and environmental goals. Manufacturing firms must be creative and flexible to remain profitable and environmentally friendly. 5. Research Implications Strategic I4.0 integration for business BUSU: The research emphasises the BUSU benefits of I4.0 technology when linked with ORIN and continuous development. I4.0 is a technology improvement and a strategy that includes structural changes, new business models, and adaptable processes that manufacturing businesses must consider, including a technical update. Businesses that adopt an integrated strategy are more likely to develop environmentally friendly solutions that enhance both operational resilience and profitability. It might help highly competitive firms become more sustainable. Companies should invest in modern technology and rigorous process changes, as this harmony optimises environmental, operational, and financial benefits. Double Mastery of Enhancement and Innovation: Environmentalists should adopt creative management and engage in continuous learning. The research highlights that an ideal BUSU stems from concept enhancement and improvement. Leading improvement cycles and effectively using IoT and artificial intelligence should be done by practitioners. Users should create a culture that honours significant discoveries and minor, statistically based improvements. By leveraging the encouragement of experimentation and feedback in the workplace, practitioners can optimise I4.0 technology and sustain long-term advantages in operational and environmental outcomes. With an eye on this duality—innovation and COIM—programs for training and development may enable teams and departments to reinforce their culture. Researching I4.0 Sector-Specific BUSU Applications, The paper highlights the necessity of more thorough research on the reactions of several industry sectors to I4.0 projects. Future studies might examine which technologies and approaches from COIM yield the most outstanding sustainable outcomes across various manufacturing sectors. This would allow I4.0 applications to maximise BUSU in a context-sensitive manner. Longitudinal Research on Extended Impact The research underlines the importance of continuous development to optimise the benefits of I4.0 innovations over time. Researchers should consider the long-term implications of integrated I4.0 and COIM initiatives as a top priority. Such studies would give accurate statistics on the flexibility and lifetime of these combined strategies, enhancing the field. Policymakers may play a significant role in offering incentives for businesses to adopt I4.0 technology, particularly through COIM plans aimed at BUSU. This study suggests that government policies supporting innovation and process optimisation might accelerate industry-wide acceptance, resulting in group environmental benefits. Targeting green technologies and process improvement initiatives, along with incentives or tax advantages, might motivate companies to prioritise these dual goals. Developing Guidelines for Sustainable I4.0 Approaches: Policymakers can establish industry-wide standards, given the emphasis of the research on the overall performance of ORIN and its ongoing development. Manufacturers can evaluate their initiatives using regulations that define sustainable I4.0 practices or emerging certification schemes, thereby helping lawmakers encourage accountability and achieve alignment with environmental goals. This ensures a level playing field for businesses operating globally. JSON: Name: industry4_0_orin_coim_busu_sem Title: Structural equation modeling of Industry 4.0 adoption, organisational innovation, and continuous improvement effects on business sustainability in manufacturing firms in emerging economies Short Hypothesis: Higher adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies causally increases the positive effect of organisational innovation and continuous improvement on business sustainability outcomes in manufacturing firms. Related Work: Empirical work on Industry 4.0 has emphasized technical capabilities (IoT, AI, additive manufacturing, cyber-physical systems) and their potential to improve efficiency; managerial research has examined organisational innovation (ORIN) and continuous improvement (COIM) separately, using lean/TQM frameworks and incremental improvement methods. Prior empirical studies typically use cross-sectional surveys, case studies of large firms, or technology-focused performance metrics and analyze relationships with linear regression or PLS-SEM. Comparative strengths: technical studies provide objective performance traces but lack organizational mediators; managerial studies identify culture/process drivers but frequently rely on self-reported outcomes. Limitations across the literature include: (1) sparse integration of I4.0, ORIN, and COIM in unified causal models; (2) limited mediation/moderation analyses that quantify how I4.0 alters ORIN→BUSU or COIM→BUSU paths; (3) underrepresentation of SMEs and emerging-economy firms; (4) reliance on subjective sustainability indicators with few studies using objective energy/waste metrics; (5) predominance of cross-sectional designs preventing causal inference; and (6) insufficient sector-specific comparative analyses. Abstract: This research tests whether Industry 4.0 adoption strengthens the causal effect of organisational innovation and continuous improvement on business sustainability (economic, environmental, social) in manufacturing firms in emerging economies. We propose a structural equation modeling (SEM) pipeline that combines validated survey measures of ORIN, COIM, and perceived BUSU with objective operational metrics (energy use, waste, production output, financial performance) and an Industry 4.0 maturity index. The main contribution is an empirical decomposition of direct, indirect (mediated), and moderated pathways: (a) ORIN → BUSU, (b) COIM as mediator, and (c) Industry 4.0 maturity as a moderator of these paths. The expected outcome is quantified evidence of whether and how technology adoption amplifies organisational drivers of sustainability, plus model fit and predictive estimates usable by managers and policymakers. Results will identify which pathways explain variance in sustainability outcomes and whether effects differ by firm size and sector. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary survey of N=200–400 manufacturing firms in an emerging-economy region capturing Likert-scale items for ORIN (innovation adoption, managerial support, R&D processes), COIM (lean/Six Sigma practices, PDCA usage), perceived BUSU (economic, environmental, social subscales), and Industry 4.0 maturity checklist. (2) Operational records linked to survey respondents for the prior 12 months: energy consumption (kWh), waste generated (kg), production volume (units), downtime (hours), and financial indicators (revenue, operating margin). Preprocessing: missing data handled via multiple imputation (m=20), variables standardized, outliers winsorized at 1st/99th percentiles. Baselines: (A) OLS multiple regression predicting BUSU from ORIN and COIM with controls; (B) PLS-SEM (predictive-focused); (C) CB-SEM full measurement + structural model (primary method); (D) machine-learning predictive baseline (random forest) using same features to compare predictive accuracy. Model specification: measurement model validated by EFA then CFA; reliability: Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability; convergent/discriminant validity: AVE and HTMT. Hypothesis tests: direct paths ORIN→BUSU, COIM→BUSU estimated; mediation ORIN→COIM→BUSU tested via bootstrap (5,000 resamples) producing bias-corrected 95% CIs; moderation of ORIN→BUSU by Industry4.0 maturity tested via (i) interaction term in SEM and (ii) multigroup SEM across terciles of maturity. Evaluation metrics: SEM fit indices (CFI≥0.95, TLI≥0.95, RMSEA≤0.06, SRMR≤0.08), standardized path coefficients (β), p-values, R2 of endogenous constructs, indirect effect size and % mediation, AIC/BIC for model comparison, out-of-sample predictive RMSE and MAE (10-fold cross-validation) for predictive baselines, Q2 predictive relevance for PLS. Ablation/comparison studies: (1) remove Industry4.0 moderator and compare path coefficients and fit indices; (2) remove COIM mediator to quantify change in ORIN→BUSU direct effect; (3) run models using subjective BUSU only vs objective operational BUSU metrics; (4) subgroup analyses SMEs vs large firms and sector-specific multigroup SEM (automotive, electronics, heavy machinery). Reporting: standardized estimates with 95% bootstrap CIs, chi-square difference tests for nested models, and effect-size Cohen's f2 for key predictors. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-reported survey measures introduce common-method and social-desirability bias; objective operational data may be unavailable or inconsistently measured across firms, producing missing-not-at-random patterns. Cross-sectional design limits causal inference and distinguishes association from causation; reverse causality or simultaneity (sustainable firms being more likely to adopt I4.0) can bias path estimates. Sample size (N≈200) may be insufficient for highly parameterized CB-SEM models or extensive multigroup tests, reducing statistical power. Measurement noninvariance across sectors or firm sizes can invalidate pooled SEM results. Multicollinearity among ORIN, COIM, and Industry 4.0 indicators can inflate standard errors and obscure unique effects. Endogeneity from omitted variables (e.g., management quality, access to capital) can bias coefficients. Operational metrics (energy, waste) may be influenced by product mix or reporting practices, limiting comparability. Findings from a single emerging-economy region may not generalize to other geographies or large multinational firms. Extensive bootstrap resampling and model estimation may require nontrivial compute resources and careful convergence diagnostics. Ethical/privacy constraints may restrict linkage of survey responses to operational records for some firms.
